A repository without .mailmap, without .git-blame-ignore-revs, or without review history is incomplete even when the owners that were scored look confident. The summary lists each reason. Missing evidence lowers evidence quality. It does not lower the ownership score, and it is not reported as drift.

--fail-on-incomplete, or policy.incomplete_analysis.fail: true, exits 3 when the score is below 1. Leave it off until the repository can satisfy the sources you care about. --exit-zero still turns that 3 into 0.

docs.title: What exit code should a script check?
docs.text:
Code Meaning 0 Clean, or findings hidden by --exit-zero 1 Internal error 2 Configuration or usage error 3 Findings (validate, drift, expired suppressions, incomplete analysis) 4 Git or GitHub integration failure

Any non-zero status fails the step. The Action exits 3 when a novel finding's policy check fails. The default policy blocks invalid owners and does not block drift, a single expert, or unowned paths, so a one-person repository with a valid CODEOWNERS file stays green. fail_on_drift: "true" blocks novel drift for that run. --exit-zero and fail_on_drift: "false" hide findings only. The full table is in Exit codes.

docs.title: Why is the first run on a small repository not a red X?
docs.text: Knowledge risk takes time to fix. The default policy reports single-expert paths, ownership drift, and missing coverage, and it does not fail the job for them. A broken owner token or a CODEOWNERS syntax error still exits 3. Set policy.drift.fail: true when the repository is ready to block on new drift. A baseline still decides which findings are new, and policy decides which of those new findings block. Both show up in the summary.

docs.title: Is this a performance-measurement tool?
docs.text: No. This is a knowledge-risk tool, not a performance-measurement tool. Using it for individual evaluation is unsupported and harmful. The project will not be positioned around who contributes least, who is really working, or which engineer is underperforming. Position it around repository resilience, knowledge continuity, review routing, organizational alignment, and onboarding. The ten principles are in Methodology. What repository evidence cannot prove is in Limitations. What is read, what leaves the machine, and how to delete the cache are in Privacy.

docs.title: How does CheckOwners compare to other CODEOWNERS tools?
docs.text:
CheckOwners treats code ownership as a scored spectrum rather than a static binary declaration. No other open-source tool combines git-history inference, per-path ownership scores with evidence quality, pattern-aware drift with severity tiers, and knowledge-risk reporting behind a single CI-native JSON contract.

Dedicated validators still go further on owner validity: they verify that accounts exist and that users and teams belong to the organization. Formal bus/truck-factor research tools run a removal simulation over a knowledge distribution. CheckOwners qualified_owner_count is a capped count of owners above the confidence threshold; it is not truck factor, bus factor, or lottery factor. See Qualified owner count and Knowledge concentration.

The full matrix and what each category does well live in How checkowners compares.

docs.title: Why did scores used to change overnight with no commits?
docs.text: Recency used to age against the wall clock, so the same commit scored differently each day. Analysis now uses one instant: --as-of, else SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH, else the HEAD committer timestamp. The same repository, commit, and config produce the same JSON. Pass --as-of 2026-01-15T00:00:00+00:00 to pin an audit instant. --deterministic is the documented name for that guarantee.

docs.title: Does CheckOwners use LLMs?
docs.text: No LLM is in the inference path. Core analysis is deterministic git work (git log, git blame) plus optional GitHub API lookups. The scoring heuristics live in analyze.py and are auditable. The codebase has been built with agent assistance; every AI-assisted change is human-reviewed, tested, and signed off.

docs.title: How do I report a wrong owner?
docs.text: Open a false-positive report. The form asks for the path, inferred owner, expected owner, command, configuration, repository shape, and merge strategy. Those reports feed the public false-positive ledger. Crashes and CLI defects use the bug form. Usage questions go to Discussions.

docs.title: Can I keep a hand-written rule when I generate CODEOWNERS?
docs.text: Yes. Put the rule between # checkowners:manual:start and # checkowners:manual:end. Regeneration copies that block unchanged and rewrites only the generated block. The file still needs the machine-generated header, or --force on the first write. A file with no markers is still refused without --force.

docs.title: Which block wins when a manual rule and a generated rule match the same path?
docs.text: The later block wins. output.block_order: manual-first (the default) places the manual block first, so the generated rule wins the overlap. generated-first places the manual block last, so the manual rule wins. Drift reports that manual winner as declared ownership without observed expertise and asks for review. It does not call the rule changed.

docs.title: Why did generate stop on a marker error and leave the file alone?
docs.text: A marker is missing its partner, repeated, or nested inside the other block. Generate exits 2 and does not write. Close the block, or remove the extra marker, and run again.

docs.title: What does drift --fix-plan change?
docs.text: Nothing. It prints a suggested diff for generated rules and a review sentence for manual rules. It does not write CODEOWNERS and it does not open a pull request.

docs.title: Why did generate warn about routes/[id]/ and emit per-file rules?
docs.text: GitHub skips CODEOWNERS lines that contain [...] character ranges, so Next.js and Remix dynamic segments cannot be written as-is. Generate rewrites those segments to *. When that wildcard would also own paths that were inferred for someone else (routes/[slug]/, routes/static/), the default is to refuse the broad rule, warn, and emit per-file rules. Those per-file lines stay GitHub-valid when a narrower * is unique; otherwise they keep the literal [id] path, which GitHub will ignore. Pass --allow-broad-patterns (or set output.allow_broad_patterns: true) only when you accept that over-ownership. --force does not opt in. generate --json records the affected paths and owner delta under broad_patterns.

docs.title: generate failed with a round-trip verification error.
docs.text: The generated rules did not resolve to the owners generation assigned. The message names the path, the intended owners, the resolved owners, and the winning rule. Last-match-wins ordering is the usual cause: a later broader rule (for example *) un-owns a subtree that a directory rule was meant to cover. Fix the ordering, or set output.consolidate: false and regenerate. A manual block that wins the path is kept and is not this error. --force does not skip this check. checkowners explain-path <path> shows the match chain for a single path.

docs.title: generate refused because the file is too large.
docs.text: GitHub does not load a CODEOWNERS file over 3 MB. Generate warns at 2 MB and refuses above output.max_bytes (default 2_500_000) unless you pass --force. Consolidation (output.consolidate: true) is the usual way to stay under the ceiling.

docs.title: How do I see which CODEOWNERS rule owns a path?
docs.text:
checkowners explain-path src/main.py
checkowners explain-path src/main.py --json

The command reads the existing CODEOWNERS file and lists every matching rule in file order. The last match wins. It does not re-run analysis.

docs.title: How do I see why someone was inferred (or not) for a path?
docs.text: checkowners explain-path answers the declared-rule question. checkowners explain PATH answers the inference question: per-signal scores, availability, named commits, and --why-not @handle. checkowners owners PATH (or who) prints only the ranked list. Those two commands analyze the requested path only and do not use the cached state.

docs.title: networkx is not installed but I want checkowners graph.
docs.text: Install the extra: pip install "checkowners[graph]". The error message points to this too.

docs.title: checkowners drift complains about lines with # alice(0.92).
docs.text: You're on an older version that predates the inline-comment fix. Upgrade to v0.3.0+ or strip the annotations by setting output.include_confidence: false and regenerating.

docs.title: The qualified-owners report says every path has one qualified owner. Is that right?
docs.text: For a solo-maintainer repo, yes. qualified_owner_count is the number of selected owners with confidence at or above analysis.confidence_threshold, after the list has already been truncated to analysis.top_n_owners (default 3). A single committer is 1 per path. The value cannot exceed top_n_owners, so fifteen healthy contributors report the same count as three. This capped count is not truck factor. checkowners simulate --remove is the removal: it reports the repository truck factor before and after the named people leave. Per-path JSON reports score-mass concentration, computed before that cap, as risk.top_owner_share, risk.effective_owners (1 / sum(p_i^2)), risk.truck_factor_50, risk.truck_factor_75, and risk.truck_factor_90. The repository figure is the criticality-weighted distribution of top_owner_share (minimum, p10, median, p90, critical_path_risk, knowledge_at_risk). Without a criticality map, distribution.criticality_incomplete is true. Changing top_n_owners does not change the concentration numbers. See Qualified owner count. The composite Action does not open a knowledge-risk PR comment for the solo-maintainer case: single-owner paths are expected when only one human has qualified ownership.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
One sentence for each term used in reports. Naming rules are in Terminology.

  • analysis completeness: the fraction of the evidence catalog that a run actually collected.
  • baseline: an accepted-findings file that later runs compare against, so they fail only on new findings.
  • candidate backup reviewer: another scored person on a path, listed after the primary owners as someone who could review it.
  • CODEOWNERS: the committed file that names who should review each path.
  • confidence delta: the clamped gap on one path between the owners declared in CODEOWNERS and the owners inferred from history.
  • continuity risk: a freshness status of inactive, superseded, or departed for a scored owner. stable means the gap fits the path and is not a warning.
  • critical-path risk: the criticality-weighted mean of top-owner share across the reported paths.
  • criticality: a configured weight in (0, 1] for a path glob, used when aggregating repository risk.
  • drift: a comparison of inferred owners with the committed CODEOWNERS rules, reported with a severity and a maximum score gap.
  • effective owners: the inverse Herfindahl index of ownership-score shares on a path, 1 / sum(p_i^2), computed before top_n_owners truncation.
  • evidence quality: a separate measure of how much configured signal weight was observed, multiplied by analysis completeness, and never folded into the ownership score.
  • exploratory repository topology: an experimental Louvain clustering of contributors from weighted co-ownership, not an org chart.
  • git authorship proxy: commit totals reported when recorded reviews are unavailable. They are not review load and they do not recommend a person.
  • load signal: the label on a balance report: github_completed_reviews, git_authorship_proxy, or external.
  • review concentration: one person's share of reviews on a single path, reported when that share is at least 0.72 and at least two owners meet the confidence threshold.
  • HHI: the Herfindahl index of ownership-score shares on a path, the sum of the squared shares.
  • historical activity confidence: the trends series historical_activity_confidence, the mean top score at a period end from recency and frequency only (historical-v1). It is not ownership_score.
  • historical confidence: the present ownership_score stored on a continuity-risk warning (historical_confidence). It is not the trends series.
  • knowledge at risk: the share of criticality weight on paths whose qualified owner count is at or below the critical threshold.
  • last match wins: the CODEOWNERS rule that the last matching pattern in file order assigns the owners.
  • major contributor: a contributor whose ownership-score share on a path is at least 0.05.
  • minor contributor share: the combined ownership-score share of contributors below 0.05 on a path.
  • ownership graph: contributors, files, directories, the repository, teams, and CODEOWNERS rules, linked by the relations current evidence can support.
  • ownership score: a ranking from 0.0 to 1.0 built from the signals that were available, not a calibrated probability.
  • qualified owner count: the number of owners on a path at or above the confidence threshold after the list is truncated to top_n_owners, which is a capped count and not a truck factor.
  • Shannon entropy: the entropy, in nats, of the ownership-score shares on a path.
  • top owner share: the largest ownership-score share on a path.
  • truck factor: on one path, the smallest number of highest-share contributors whose scores sum to a configured fraction of inferred knowledge. The repository truck factor, from simulate, is the number of authors whose departure drops file coverage below the first truck-factor threshold.

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text: How CheckOwners turns git history into an ownership ranking. This page is the scoring contract. It is not a validation study: the score is a ranking signal, not a calibrated probability.

docs.title: Signals
docs.text:
For contributor u on path p:

Signal Meaning Available when Recency Exponential decay from last commit. scoring.recency_strategy: adaptive (default) sets the half-life to the path's median inter-commit gap, clamped to recency_half_life_floor_days and recency_half_life_ceiling_days (14 and 730). No positive gap falls back to recency_half_life_days (90). fixed uses that value for every path. Aged against the analysis instant (HEAD committer time by default, never the wall clock) The owner has a last-commit timestamp Frequency Weighted commit credit on the path inside the lookback, divided by that path's maximum credit plus prior. The commit author adds 1. A credited Co-authored-by trailer adds git.co_author_weight (default 1) when git.count_co_authors is on. Emails come from git log after .mailmap when identity.mailmap is on. prior is 3 when qualification.strategy is adaptive, and 0 when it is threshold. The commits field counts appearances. At the default weight it matches the numerator Commit counts exist for the path Blame Share of current lines git blame (porcelain, -w, .mailmap when identity.mailmap is on, and -M/-C when git.detect_moves) attributes to u. Commits listed in a resolved ignore-revs file, and mass-refactor commits above git.mass_refactor_file_fraction, are omitted so the prior author keeps the line Blame ran and produced lines for the path Review Share of PR reviews on p from pulls closed inside analysis.review_lookback_days. When that key is omitted, the window is analysis.lookback_days, including adaptive A review provider was injected (github.api_enabled plus token and GITHUB_REPOSITORY)

An author missing from a successful blame map, or from a provider result, scores 0.0 with the signal still available. That is measured zero, not missing evidence. Blame that failed or was skipped, and a run with no review provider, mark those signals unavailable.

Blame line counts are cached by blob SHA and path, together with the blame flags, the ignore-revs file bytes, the mass-refactor revision list, and the .mailmap bytes. The path is part of the key so two files with the same bytes keep their own line attribution. A hit rebuilds the same author fractions from those integer counts. The cache survives a rejected incremental baseline. Its files share the 256 MiB cap with state and graph files and are evicted oldest-first with them. --no-cache does not read or write it.

analyze and audit blame every qualified path. owners, explain, and change blame only the requested path. --diff-only blames the changed paths. risk and bus-factor reports keep the full map. The blame command stays git blame --line-porcelain, one path per process. The timed alternatives are in the benchmark readme.

docs.title: What each signal proxies
docs.text:
Signal It measures It proxies for It does not establish Recency Days since the last commit, with exponential half-life decay relative to the path's own cadence unless strategy is fixed How fresh the contact with the path is What the person knows, availability, or current employment Frequency Share of weighted commit credit on the path inside the lookback window Repeated authorship Ownership, or that a squash-merge author wrote the lines Blame Share of current lines attributed to the person Who the current text is attributed to, after whitespace, move, and ignore-revs corrections Authority to decide, or that a formatter did not touch the file Review Share of recorded pull-request reviews on pulls closed in the review window Review participation when a provider returned data Organizational accountability, or that the person is the right reviewer now

A high ownership_score is a ranking of that evidence. It is not a probability that the person should own the path.

docs.title: Ownership score
docs.text:
Missing evidence is not negative evidence. Unavailable signals are omitted and the remaining weights are renormalized so the attainable range is [0, 1] in every configuration:

ownership_score = Σ(wᵢ × aᵢ × sᵢ) / Σ(wᵢ × aᵢ)

wᵢ is the configured weight, aᵢ ∈ {0, 1} is availability, and sᵢ is the per-signal score. If no signal is available the score is 0.0. Default weights are 0.30 / 0.20 / 0.20 / 0.15 / 0.15 for recency, frequency, blame, review, and change survival.

analyze and trends share one helper. trends emits historical-v1 with signals recency and frequency. Blame and review stay unavailable, so the formula renormalizes over those two signals. That score is historical_activity_confidence, not ownership_score.

JSON from analyze emits ownership_score. analysis.confidence_threshold still gates this number.

The score is an interpretation of stored observations. Each analyzed path keeps the commit, blame, and review facts that score_owners already used: commit count, last commit, credit, cadence, blame share, and review fraction. A later scoring pass rebuilds those inputs from the stored facts and calls score_owners again. Changing a weight does not require another git or API pass. Command JSON does not add these records. They stay on the library object and in the state file.

docs.title: Evidence quality
docs.text:
Evidence quality is a separate quantity and is never folded into the score:

signal_quality = Σ(wᵢ × aᵢ × rᵢ) / Σ(wᵢ)
evidence_quality = signal_quality × analysis_completeness

rᵢ is scoring.*_reliability (default 1.0 for every signal). With those defaults, signal_quality equals the fraction of configured weight that was observed. Unavailable review therefore lowers quality (by 0.15 by default) without pulling the owner's score toward zero. analysis_completeness is the fraction of the evidence catalog that was collected (shallow history, token, review history, rate limit, budgets, team membership, identity, exclusions, renames, mailmap, ignore-revs). It is recomputed from the signal breakdown whenever gaps change, so the run score is applied once. A missing signal stays unavailable. A measured zero stays zero. The ownership score is not multiplied.

On a fresh analyze, that quality is then multiplied once by identity certainty: 1.0 when the link is an override, a noreply address, a commit login, or an already-resolved handle; 0.75 for an unresolved email; 0.5 for a user-search hit. A cached load does not scale again. Qualification still uses ownership_score, so the factor does not change who counts as an owner.

An author with at least 20 commits whose subjects are at least 80 percent one template, after commit SHAs and version numbers are stripped, or who matches a mechanical subject prefix (bump, chore(deps), dependabot, automated), keeps recency and has frequency credit capped at one commit. The author stays in the map. bots.exclude is what drops a bot address before scoring.

Human output shows both values as handle (score/quality), for example @alice 0.91/0.93 versus @bob 0.79/0.31.

contributor_status is separate from freshness status. former is set only by contributors.roster. former_knowledge_share is the share of positive ownership_score held by those owners. It is a knowledge-risk figure, not a performance measure. The knowledge-risk notice still applies.

checkowners explain PATH prints the same weighted mean as analyze. Each row shows the five signals with their configured weight and availability. A measured zero (author absent from a successful blame or review map) is a number. An unavailable signal is omitted from the mean and shown as n/a. The printed total equals Σ(wᵢ × aᵢ × sᵢ) / Σ(wᵢ × aᵢ) on the displayed tuples. --why-not uses that same total against analysis.confidence_threshold.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
Three model ids are stamped on JSON output and on human reports:

Id Config key What it names ownership-v2 model.ownership The renormalized score in this page risk-v1 model.risk Inverse-Herfindahl concentration and the qualified-owner classifier topology-v2 model.topology Weighted Louvain clusters

A formula change, a classifier change, or a topology-algorithm change bumps the matching id. That bump is a breaking change for anyone gating CI on a threshold, even when the JSON shape is unchanged. A config pin must equal the id this release implements, or be omitted. Cached analyze state and the graph cache are reused only when all three ids match.

JSON carries models.ownership, models.risk, and models.topology. Per-repo state is schema 1. Email addresses in that state are stored as tokens.

Files without a matching models object, and files whose scoring config hash does not match, are ignored and replaced on the next analyze. A cached map is reused only when its commit is still HEAD, unless --allow-stale is set. When the stored commit is an ancestor of HEAD and the baseline is usable, the next analyze replays git log metadata for the current lookback, attaches stored path lists for commits it already saw, and re-blames only paths whose blob changed. Commits that git log --since and --until no longer return are left out of the map. The scored result is the same function of the repository, commit, config, and model as a full lookback. --no-incremental forces that full lookback. Recency and the lookback window are evaluated at the analysis instant, not the wall clock. JSON payloads emit head_sha and generated_at.

qualification.strategy: adaptive (the default) treats commit count as evidence: authors below min_commits still qualify when blame is at least strong_blame_override. strategy: threshold keeps the previous eligibility gate and the undamped commits / max_commits frequency ratio.

Weight search has not been run. See Benchmark and calibration.

docs.title: Knowledge concentration
docs.text:
qualified_owner_count is the number of owners on a path whose ownership_score is at or above analysis.confidence_threshold, taken from the list already truncated to analysis.top_n_owners (default 3). JSON emits qualified_owner_count and qualified_owner_count_cap. Human output states the cap. Raising top_n_owners raises the maximum reportable count without any code changing hands.

Before that rename, the same count was labeled bus factor. It was a qualified-owner count, not a removal simulation. The count is unchanged. The bus_factor config section classifies the capped count.

Concentration uses every contributor at or above analysis.confidence_threshold, before top_n_owners truncation. The displayed owner list is still truncated. Expertise is ownership_score. A survival-weighted score is not part of this model. Shares are not a JSON key. For each positive score on that untruncated list:

p_i = score_i / sum(score)
top_owner_share = max(p_i)
hhi = sum(p_i^2)
effective_owners = 1 / hhi
shannon_entropy = -sum(p_i * ln(p_i))
truck_factor_50 = smallest k whose largest shares sum to at least q_50
truck_factor_75 = smallest k whose largest shares sum to at least q_75
truck_factor_90 = smallest k whose largest shares sum to at least q_90

q_50, q_75, and q_90 are risk.truck_factor_thresholds, default [0.50, 0.75, 0.90], in that order. The array is repeated on the risk object. shannon_entropy is in nats. hhi is the Herfindahl index on the unit interval. effective_owners is the inverse Herfindahl index: one owner is 1.00, an even split of two is 2.00, and four equal shares are 4.00. It is not the exponential of Shannon entropy.

A contributor is major when p_i >= 0.05. major_contributor_count is that count. minor_contributor_share is the sum of the other shares. The 5% line is fixed.

An empty or all-zero list reports top_owner_share 0.0, effective_owners 0.0, shannon_entropy 0.0, hhi 0.0, minor_contributor_share 0.0, major_contributor_count 0, and truck factors 0.

These truck factors are coverage counts on one path's score mass. They are not a repository truck factor. checkowners simulate --remove is that repository removal: it drops named people from the cached map and reports files that lose their only author, files left with one author, fully orphaned directories, and the repository truck factor before and after. Changing top_n_owners changes the displayed list and qualified_owner_count. It does not change concentration. The bus_factor config section still classifies the capped count: critical at or below critical_threshold, warning at or below warn_threshold.

Repository output does not average that capped count. It distributes top_owner_share after weighting each path by criticality. The first matching glob wins. An unmatched path weighs 1.0. An empty map uses that weight and sets criticality_incomplete, because risk without a criticality map is incomplete. Weighted percentiles of top_owner_share are minimum, p10, median, and p90, taken as the first share whose cumulative weight reaches the quantile. critical_path_risk is sum(weight * top_owner_share) / sum(weight). knowledge_at_risk is the share of total weight on paths whose qualified_owner_count is at or below critical_threshold.

docs.title: Composite risk
docs.text:
checkowners risk ranks paths by a 0-100 score. bus-factor and decay are aliases of that command. qualified-owners still reports the capped count. The score is the geometric mean of the factors that are present:

risk = round(100 * exp(mean(ln(factor))))

Each factor is in (0, 1]. A missing factor is left out of the mean. It is not replaced with 1.

Factor Meaning ownership_concentration top_owner_share on the untruncated scored owners. No positive score is 1.0. change_frequency 1 / (1 + cadence_days / 7). One recorded change is 0.05. Missing change_events leaves the factor out. dependency_criticality Co-change degree divided by the repository maximum. Commits that touch more than 20 files are ignored. No partner leaves the factor out. code_criticality The first matching criticality glob. Otherwise 0.8 for a deploy or manifest path (Dockerfile, docker-compose*.yml, compose*.yml, Chart.yaml, a k8s or deploy directory, *.tf, Procfile, fly.toml, serverless.yml). Otherwise left out. expertise_decay 1 - the dominant owner's active_expertise, and at least 0.05. No freshness leaves the factor out.

criticality_unavailable is true when the repository has no criticality map, no manifest or deploy path, and no co-change degree. The report says repository risk is incomplete without criticality. The qualified-owner distribution still uses weight 1.0 and criticality_incomplete in that case.

Tiers on the 0-100 score are critical at or above 75, high at or above 50, medium at or above 25, and low otherwise. reason names the strong factors: single expert, high churn, dependency criticality, stale expertise, low criticality.

Four pathologies are findings, suppressible by baseline rule and path:

Rule When knowledge-vacuum The best score is below analysis.confidence_threshold, or every owner at that threshold is inactive, superseded, or departed. phantom-ownership A CODEOWNERS owner has no commits and no review signal on the path. The detail is declared ownership without observed expertise. Skipped when handles and emails cannot be compared. shadow-maintainer A declared owner exists and the dominant observed expert is a different identity. ownership-review-divergence The writer, the reviewer, and the declared owner are three different identities. Omitted when review evidence is unavailable.

Observed ownership coverage is the share of analyzed paths with qualified_owner_count >= 1. Critical components are paths in the critical tier. High CODEOWNERS drift counts drift entries with confidence_delta >= 0.7, or with qualified_owner_count at or below bus_factor.critical_threshold, or with decay set.

docs.title: Prior art
docs.text:
Published truck factor, also called bus factor or lottery factor, is the smallest set of people whose departure leaves a project, or a threshold fraction of its files, without a knowledgeable author.

Avelino, Passos, Hora, and Valente, "A Novel Approach for Estimating Truck Factors" (ICPC 2016, arXiv:1604.06766), estimate degree of authorship per file, keep authors above a normalized threshold, then greedily remove the author who covers the most files until at least half the files have no remaining author. Ferreira, Valente, and Ferreira, "A Comparison of Three Algorithms for Computing Truck Factors" (ICPC 2017), compare that algorithm with the blame-based estimate of Rigby et al. and the file-then-project estimate of Cosentino et al.

Degree of knowledge, Fritz, Ou, Murphy, and Murphy-Hill (ICSE 2010) and Fritz, Murphy, Murphy-Hill, Ou, and Hill, "Degree-of-Knowledge: Modeling a Developer's Knowledge of Code" (TOSEM 2014), adds interaction (reviews, navigation) to authorship. CheckOwners does not compute degree of authorship or degree of knowledge. simulate removes people from the existing author sets (scores at or above the confidence threshold). It does not compute DOA.

The divergence is deliberate. The old headline number was the capped qualified_owner_count. Calling it bus factor overclaimed the literature. CheckOwners reports per-path knowledge shares, inverse-Herfindahl effective_owners, and truck_factor_50, truck_factor_75, and truck_factor_90 over every score above the confidence threshold. Those counts remove the highest-knowledge contributors on one path until a share of inferred knowledge is gone. The repository truck factor, reported by simulate, greedily removes the author who still covers the most files until covered files drop below the first risk.truck_factor_thresholds value (default 0.50). That coverage line is the one in Avelino et al. Ties break by identity so the count is stable.

docs.title: Exploratory repository topology
docs.text:
checkowners topology is experimental. It is a hypothesis about repository collaboration, not an org chart and not a team assignment.

The person graph is weighted. Co-ownership adds min(confidence) for each shared path where both people clear analysis.confidence_threshold. Co-review adds min(review score) only when both review signals are available. A missing review is left out, not stored as zero. Shared-module activity adds 0.25 for each parent directory where both people qualify on at least one file. Co-change and temporal collaboration are not available: cochange_degree counts files that change together, and last_commit is not a shared time window. The report names those signals as unavailable. Co-review is unavailable when no shared path has a review score.

Clusters come from Louvain (networkx.community.louvain_partitions), seed 0, resolution 1.0 unless --resolution is set. Values above 1 favor smaller clusters. Modularity uses that same resolution and the primary partition. Stability is the mean and population variance of greedy Jaccard matches across seeds 0 through 4. Stability is unavailable when the person graph has no edges.

Louvain returns a partition. A person is also listed on another cluster when their edge weight into it is at least half their weight into the primary cluster and they connect to at least two of its members. One bridge edge does not affiliate. members is the primary partition. affiliated_members is the extra membership. When Louvain emits more than one level, a finer cluster records the coarser community as parent.

Each declared team is compared with the closest inferred cluster, using primary and affiliated members. Jaccard is |intersection| / |union|. Precision is |intersection| / |inferred|. Recall is |intersection| / |declared|. Coverage is the share of declared members who appear in any cluster. A cluster takes a declared name only when that Jaccard is 1. People in the inferred cluster who are not on the declared team are reported as potential cross-team experts.

networkx stays an optional extra and is imported only when the run has qualified owners.

docs.title: Ownership graph
docs.text:
The ownership graph is undirected. Several relations between the same pair are one edge whose relations value is a sorted list of names. Attribute values are strings, integers, floats, or booleans.

Populated nodes are contributors, files, directories, the repository, teams, and CODEOWNERS rules. Populated edges are OWNS_OBSERVED, AUTHORED when commits > 0, REVIEWS when a review score exists, DECAYING_EXPERTISE when contributor status is former or freshness is inactive or departed, OWNS_DECLARED from parsed CODEOWNERS, MEMBER_OF, CONTAINS, and DEPENDS_ON for a Python import or from ... import that resolves to a file already in the ownership map. Installed packages are not followed. Zero resolved edges means the dependency graph is unavailable.

Not populated, because this repository has no source for them: Package, Service, Commit, PullRequest, Review, Incident, Domain, and the edges KNOWS, MODIFIES, REPLACES, and REVIEWED_BY.

Articulation points and betweenness use the unweighted ownership edges between contributors and files. Weight is a strength, so betweenness does not treat it as distance. Orphan files are those with no qualified owner outside former and inactive and whose freshness is not inactive or departed. A missing roster (unknown) does not mark the repository orphaned. A file that imports an orphan is recorded on that orphan. --from and --to print a shortest path across people and files.

docs.title: Onboarding suggestions
docs.text:
checkowners onboard is experimental. The steps are inferred suggestions. Dependency order comes from the Python edges above, prerequisites first. A cycle is named and those members use path order. When no edge resolves, dependency order is listed as unavailable.

Within a rank the sort is qualified-owner count, then change_events when present, then a matching criticality weight when present, then path. Missing values are not filled with zero. easy, medium, and hard record position in the list. The sentence on each step is the claim. Code complexity, test coverage, and documentation coverage are always named as unavailable. Domain criticality is unavailable when no configured rule matches a selected path.

Mentor candidates are qualified owners on the selected steps except former, inactive, and bot. Rank is the number of those steps that have another qualified owner, then fewer commits, then handle. The list is capped at three and labeled as candidates.

docs.title: Terminology
docs.text:
Use these names in human-facing output. JSON keys and command names stay as shipped. Definitions are in docs/GLOSSARY.md.

Instead of Use organizational owner repository-evidence candidate, reviewer candidate, evidence-ranked reviewer expertise decay ownership freshness, evidence freshness, continuity risk backup reviewer candidate backup reviewer bus factor (as previously computed) qualified owner count, reviewer depth uncalibrated 0.92 evidence score, ranking signal, ownership score knowledge graph (as modeled) ownership graph org chart exploratory repository topology review load (from commits) git authorship proxy trend score historical activity confidence

docs.title: Never collapse these
docs.text:
• Contribution into ownership.
  • Blame into authority.
  • Recent activity into expertise.
  • Co-commit clusters into teams.
  • Inferred reviewer affinity into organizational accountability.
  • An uncalibrated score into a probability.

docs.title: Other reported numbers
docs.text:
historical_confidence is the present ownership_score stored on a continuity-risk warning. It is not historical_activity_confidence and it is not a score reconstructed at an earlier date.

active_expertise, historical_expertise, and maintenance_recency are separate evidence scores on each owner. active_expertise is the recency term: this person's last commit, decayed by the effective half-life. historical_expertise is this person's commits divided by their commits plus later commits by anyone else. maintenance_recency is the path's latest commit, decayed by the same half-life. None of the three measures what a person knows. historical_expertise counts commits. It does not measure which lines survived.

Continuity risk is a status. stable means the gap fits the path's cadence, or this person made the latest commit and the gap is within the half-life ceiling, and no warning is emitted. Change survival is current blame lines / blame lines at that person's last commit on the lineage path, clamped to [0, 1]. It is a line count from git blame, not an AST comparison. A zero denominator leaves the signal unavailable. When it is available and below 0.2, and someone else committed later, the status is superseded. When it is available and at least 0.2, later commits do not mark the owner superseded; the cadence and time rules still choose stable or inactive. When the signal is unavailable, superseded still means later commits by others outnumber this person's commits. inactive means the gap is past the cadence bound, or the path has no commit interval and the gap exceeds decay.threshold_days. departed means inactive on every path. analysis.lookback_days: adaptive keeps stable paths inside the history window.

historical_activity_confidence is the mean, across paths that still have a scored owner, of the top score at the end of one trend period. The model is historical-v1 and the signals are recency and frequency. avg_qualified_owner_count is the mean capped count for those same paths. Blame, review, and change survival are unavailable, so this number is not ownership_score (ownership-v2).

load_signal says what a balance count is. github_completed_reviews means the GitHub sample returned submitted reviews. git_authorship_proxy means it did not, and reviews in that payload is a commit total. external means the caller supplied completed-review counts. The proxy never sets reviews_completed, load_band, review_concentration, or divergence, and it never recommends a person. Commit volume is not review load.

diff and suggest --diff are routing suggestions for the changed paths. Each recommended person carries evidence_quality and the signal scores already computed for that pass (recency, frequency, blame, review when that signal was available). A high load band moves a person out of the recommended list only when load_signal is github_completed_reviews or external, and the reason includes the open-review count. The authorship proxy does not demote and does not treat commits as review load. The suggestion does not assign pull-request reviewers.

When the signal is real reviews, reviews_completed counts submitted review objects in the suggest closed-pull sample (at most 200, most recently updated). That cap is not the ownership review window. reviews_requested counts one fulfilled request per pull a person reviewed, plus each open request that has no submitted review from them. prs_waiting counts those open requests. The open scan uses the same cap. It is not a new lookback window. median_response_time_hours is the median, in hours, from pull creation to that person's earliest submitted review on the pull. It is not request-to-review time. reviewed_lines sums additions + deletions once per reviewed pull. pr_complexity is the median of those per-pull totals. ownership_criticality is the highest configured criticality weight on a path the person owns at or above the confidence threshold, or unset when none match. Per-path review counts increment once per pull that touched the path, not once per review comment.

load_band is high when completed reviews are at least twice the average, or prs_waiting is at least twice its average. It is low when the person is not high and both numbers are at or below their averages (waiting is ignored when it was not collected). Otherwise it is typical. The recommendation names one co-owner who is not high: low before typical, then higher ownership_score (expertise), then fewer completed reviews, then handle. ownership_score here is the same uncalibrated ranking signal as everywhere else.

review_concentration is the top reviewer's share of per-path reviews. It is reported when that share is at least 0.72 and at least two owners on the path meet the confidence threshold. It is not ownership concentration. divergence keeps three identities: the writer (most commits; ties break by higher score, then handle), the reviewer (most reviews on that path), and a declared CODEOWNERS owner who is neither. Missing any one of the three omits the path.

confidence_delta is the drift gap between declared CODEOWNERS owners and inferred owners on one path: the sum of inferred scores for people who are inferred but not declared, plus 1.0 for each declared owner who is not inferred, clamped to [0, 1]. max_confidence_delta is the largest absolute confidence_delta in the drift result, or 0.0 when there are no entries.

docs.title: Ownership beliefs
docs.text:
These cases are the project's stated ownership philosophy. tests/test_golden.py is the judgment suite. Each history is a real git repository with pinned author and committer dates. Analysis uses a fixed as-of of 2026-06-01T12:00:00+00:00 (the handoff reuses one repository at three earlier pinned instants). The expected sentence for each case is stored under the model id, currently ownership-v2. A model-version bump fails until that record gains the new id. A run that breaks a belief fails with the sentence.

Strong ownership in that suite means a score of at least 0.5. Medium evidence quality means a quality of at least 0.4 and below 1.

Formatting does not confer ownership. Alice creates foo.py (alongside other tracked files, so the later edit stays under the mass-refactor fraction) and edits it. Bob changes only whitespace. Alice reviews that change. Alice stays the primary expert. Bob's blame share is zero, and his score is below Alice's.

Ownership moves gradually. Alice's last commit stays inside the 365-day lookback. Bob then replaces the file in a few commits across that year. Alice is primary at the first as-of. Her score is lower at each later as-of and still above zero at the last one. Bob's score rises, and Bob is primary at the end.

A single creating commit is strong, with medium evidence. One commit that adds a file makes that author the sole primary owner. The score is strong. Evidence quality is medium, because review and other catalog gaps are missing.

A full rewrite leaves no current lines for the original author. Bob replaces every line Alice wrote. Bob is primary. Alice's blame share is zero. That share is how this model shows superseded work.

One person, one owner. Three commit addresses that .mailmap maps to one canonical email score as a single owner.

Missing blame and review stay on the unit interval. An empty tracked file produces no blame lines, and no review provider is configured, so those two signals are unavailable. The score stays inside (0, 1]. A commit still supplies frequency, so the case scores the signals that were observed.

Rename. Ownership survives a rename from foo.py to bar.py. History aggregation follows renames and copies that git reports at analysis.rename_similarity (default 50). The earlier author stays on the new path. analysis.follow_renames: false keys on the literal path again, so only the rename commit is scored on bar.py. A directory rename is one prefix move applied to every file that moved with it. A copy is linked only when the source is modified in that same commit; an untouched source starts a new file. The lineage pass on a 300-file directory rename stays within 10 seconds. Rename confidence is the lowest similarity on the chain, as a fraction, and it scales evidence quality for that path. A score of 1.0 means the path was not renamed, or every rename was exact.

Stable cadence. Intended belief: a path with an 18-month cadence keeps its owner. Under ownership-v2, a commit 18 months before the as-of falls outside the 365-day lookback and the 90-day half-life, so the path has no scored owner.

Co-authors. A Co-authored-by trailer adds a scored owner on every file in that commit. Blame stays with the commit author, so the co-author's blame share is zero. git.count_co_authors: false scores only the commit author.

When a later model makes the rename or cadence record match the intended belief, update the ownership-v2 sentences, or add the new model id, in the same change.

docs.title: Benchmark and calibration
docs.text:
Runtimes are measured by benchmarks/harness.py. A result records cold runtime, warm runtime, peak resident memory, git command count, GitHub API request count, cache size, and incremental runtime after one new commit. Peak resident memory comes from time -l on macOS and time -v on Linux. Two runs on the same commit must match the git command count exactly. Wall time within 15% is checked unless --counts-only is set. The pull-request job passes --counts-only because a hosted runner does not hold that band. A run fails the regression check when its cold time is above the recorded baseline times 1.15. The procedure and the current ci baseline are in the benchmark readme.

The J1 incremental measurement, from one development machine on 2026-10-24, used 600 one-line Python files added across 20 commits, then one commit that changed two of those files. The cold pass took 1.99 seconds and ran git blame on all 600 files. The warm pass took 0.34 seconds and ran git blame on the two changed files.

The default weights 0.30 / 0.20 / 0.20 / 0.15 / 0.15 stay in place unless a held-out comparison beats them. Ground truth is who later maintains the code. For a cutoff commit, prediction uses only history at or before that commit. The label for a path is the authors of non-merge commits that change it afterward. Reviewer labels are used only when a review provider returned reviews submitted after the cutoff. Commit counts are never labeled as reviews. When that sample is absent, review_metrics is unavailable. The committed CODEOWNERS file is not a label and is not the fit objective.

The cutoff is the commit nearest 60 percent of the way from the first commit time to the last. A re-run at the same pinned commits must match exactly. That is the variance band.

precision_at_1, precision_at_3, and precision_at_5 are the mean, over labeled paths, of the number of positive authors in the top k divided by k. recall_at_3 divides that overlap by the size of the positive set. mrr is the mean reciprocal rank of the first positive author. ndcg is binary NDCG over the full ranking, with discount log2(rank + 1). brier is the mean squared error of the top score against whether that person later changed the path. calibration_error is the expected absolute gap between bin mean score and hit rate across ten bins. changed_file_coverage is the share of labeled paths that had at least one candidate. acceptance_rate is the share of top-1 predictions that later changed the path. rejection_rate, false_positive_rate, and stale_ownership_rate are the complementary share among paths that had a prediction. Under this label those three rates are the same quantity. handoff_days is the mean days from the cutoff until a different author first holds a strict majority of later commits, on paths where that happens.

Baselines rank the same candidates by commit count, blame share, or recency alone. The published table keeps rows where a baseline wins.

Repository holdout sorts ids and reserves every fourth repository. The weight search is a 0.05 grid on the other repositories. It never sees the held-out ids. Shipped defaults change only when held-out precision_at_1 improves by at least 0.02. ownership_score is called a calibrated probability only when every occupied bin is within 0.1 of its hit rate. Otherwise the name stays ownership_score.

checkowners calibrate reports the same held-out metrics for one repository. checkowners calibrate --fit learns weights on the earliest 80 percent of labeled paths and writes the later 20 percent into .github/checkowners.yml with the cutoff, sample sizes, and held-out metrics. It refuses when history is shorter than 180 days or labeled paths are fewer than 30. Training-slice metrics are not the result. A fitted vector whose L1 distance from the shipped defaults is above 0.20 produces a warning.

The public false-positive ledger in docs/false-positives.md records a prediction, the judgment, the reason, the fix, and the evidence that produced the prediction. New reports use the false-positive issue form. Corrections use the categories recommendation_correct, recommendation_wrong, right_person_unavailable, team_owns_it, security_owner_required, compliance_owner_required, temporary_migration, departed_contributor, useful_but_incomplete, no_ownership, and should_not_own.

Published numbers for the current corpus are in benchmarks/validation_results.json. The corpus list is benchmarks/validation_corpus.json.

The held-out repositories are davegamble/cJSON, google/uuid, kjd/idna, pallets/markupsafe, and ruby/rake. That slice has 306 labeled paths and 133 paths with a candidate. ownership_score is not a calibrated probability on this slice: occupied bins are not all within 0.1 of their hit rate, and calibration_error is 0.3918.

Held-out precision_at_1 for the shipped weights is 0.3105. The best grid point on the other repositories scored 0.3039 on the same slice, which is below the 0.02 margin, so the shipped weights stayed 0.30 / 0.20 / 0.20 / 0.15 / 0.15. Ranking the same candidates by commit count scored 0.3268. Recency alone scored 0.317. Blame alone scored 0.2941. Commit count wins this slice.

The same slice: precision_at_3 0.1198, precision_at_5 0.0745, recall_at_3 0.1447, mrr 0.3316, ndcg 0.3091, brier 0.3966, changed_file_coverage 0.4346, acceptance_rate 0.7143, rejection_rate 0.2857, false_positive_rate 0.2857, stale_ownership_rate 0.2857, handoff_days 362.1566. Reviewer overload, review latency, and time to first useful review were not computed.

Held-out precision_at_1 by language: C 0.0303 (33 paths), Go 0.0 (27 paths), Python 0.15 (120 paths), Ruby 0.6032 (126 paths). JavaScript, Rust, the small monorepo, and medium-turnover repositories were in the fit and not in this held-out slice, so they have no held-out row.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
1. Evidence over guesses. Every ownership recommendation must derive from inspectable evidence.
  2. Human policy remains authoritative. Observed expertise informs CODEOWNERS. It does not silently override governance.
  3. Missing evidence is not negative evidence. Unavailable review or team information reduces evidence_quality. It does not arbitrarily depress ownership_score.
  4. Local-first. Core analysis works without uploading proprietary source.
  5. Deterministic by default. The same evidence and the same model produce the same result.
  6. Explain everything. Every score and recommendation is inspectable.
  7. Measure uncertainty. Thin evidence is not certainty. Report evidence_quality and analysis_completeness beside the score.
  8. Compatibility matters. GitHub CODEOWNERS semantics must be reproduced accurately where the pattern language is supported.
  9. No employee surveillance. The project optimizes repository resilience, knowledge continuity, review routing, organizational alignment, and onboarding. It will not be positioned around who contributes least, who is really working, or which engineer is underperforming. The data is not designed for that.
  10. Correctness before feature count. A new report waits until the number it prints is defined and bounded.

Observed expertise is evidence, not authority.

docs.title: Team comparison
docs.text:
Drift expands a team rule to people. generate does the reverse and is unchanged: it collapses people to a team.

One org team list supplies slug, parent slug, and member logins. Child links are built in memory. There is no per-team child request. A forbidden member listing marks that team invisible. A successful listing with no members and no children is empty. No token, an offline run, or a failed org list is no directory. A cached snapshot is not reread to turn that run into aligned.

Coverage for a nested team is the union of the team and its descendants. Cycles are ignored. team_coverage is the share of inferred handles who are in that set. aligned means every inferred handle is in the set. Anyone inferred outside it is partial-drift and organizational_mismatch. Members who were not inferred are inactive_members. The record stores team_snapshot from the directory timestamp.

docs.title: CODEOWNERS errors endpoint
docs.text:
GitHub's syntax source is GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/codeowners/errors?ref=. The body is {errors: [{line, column, kind, source, suggestion, message, path}]}. The local validator checks syntax and token shape. The endpoint also reports unknown users and missing access. Those owner kinds are not validator bugs.

The diff compares the syntax classes both sides own: a leading !, a pattern containing [ or ], and a malformed owner token. Other GitHub kinds are listed beside the pass rate and are not failures. A private repository, a ref other than the default branch, an empty API error list, and local syntax findings is inconclusive. That case is dropped from the pass-rate denominator. It is not counted as agreement. Doctor and audit use the same fetch and the same inconclusive check. Offline, they use the local validator and set source to local.

docs.title: Pattern semantics
docs.text:
CODEOWNERS rules are matched in file order. The last match wins. A pattern assigns owners only when it is a supported glob:

  • * stays inside one path segment. ** crosses segments.
  • A leading / anchors the pattern to the repository root. An interior / does the same. A bare name floats to any directory.
  • dir/* matches direct children of dir, not deeper files.
  • A trailing / matches files inside that directory, not a sibling whose name only shares the prefix, and not the directory path itself.
  • A line that starts with !, or a pattern that contains [ or ], does not assign an owner. A backslash before # does not turn a comment into a pattern that matches a path beginning with #.

corpus/compatibility.jsonl locks these results. A differential test compares the supported glob language (one ** segment, no leading !, no brackets, no \#) with an independent matcher. Repeated ** segments such as **/** are outside that comparison.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text:
This is a knowledge-risk tool, not a performance-measurement tool. Using it for individual evaluation is unsupported and harmful.

checkOwners reads git history on the machine where it runs and writes an ownership map. Email addresses are stored as tokens. When identity lookup is enabled, an address that is not already resolved may be sent to the GitHub user-search API. contributors.exclude keeps those people out of that lookup.

output.anonymize, output.aggregate_only, privacy.redact_emails (--redact-emails), identity.mode, and contributors.exclude control what reports may show. See Privacy controls.

suggest (alias balance) is the report most likely to be misused for individual evaluation. It names people only to recommend a reviewer. output.anonymize replaces those names with person- tokens. output.aggregate_only drops names, the recommendation, and per-person load fields, and keeps load_signal plus path-level review_concentration and divergence. Do not use either form in a performance review.

docs.title: What is read
docs.text:
All of this stays on the machine that runs the command:

  • git log and git blame (history and line attribution, not a copy of the source tree)
  • .mailmap, .git-blame-ignore-revs, and .gitattributes
  • the CODEOWNERS file, if one exists
  • .github/checkowners.yml

Source file contents are not uploaded. The cache key is the normalized origin URL, or the absolute checkout path when the repo has no origin.

docs.title: What leaves the machine
docs.text:
With --offline, with no GITHUB_TOKEN, or without the github extra, nothing does. The command prints:

Network access: disabled
Review evidence: unavailable
Team verification: unavailable

Otherwise a token can be used for the calls below. Each one runs only when its gate is on, the token is set, and the github extra is installed. --offline skips all of them. Noreply addresses, .mailmap, and an existing handle file still resolve locally.

When Call Sent github.resolve_handles is true (the default), a local commit SHA is known, and no earlier stage resolved the address GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/commits/{sha} The commit SHA. The response used is author.login, author.type, and committer.type The commit read found no login. A core rate-limit gap does not continue to this row GET /rate_limit, then GET /search/users with query {email} in:email The address is the search query. Search is last github.org is set and a token exists GET /orgs/{org}/members once per analyze The organization name. The response is member logins. A failure leaves membership unused github.api_enabled is true and GITHUB_REPOSITORY is set. Review collection also resolves handles, so the search row above can run first Ownership review: POST /graphql for closed pulls in the review window, including reviewer logins and changed paths. suggest still uses GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls (closed, newest update first, at most 200), then GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{n}/reviews and GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls/{n}/files, and reads open pulls the same way, at most 200 Repository name. Responses are reviewer logins, requested reviewers, and changed paths generate or sync with github.resolve_teams and github.org, or topology and explain when github.api_enabled and github.org are set GET /orgs/{org}, GET /orgs/{org}/teams, GET /orgs/{org}/teams/{slug}/members Organization name. Responses are team slugs and member logins Composite Action, comment_on_pr true, same-repo pull request GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/issues/{n}/comments, then POST a new comment or PATCH the existing one The report markdown checkowners sync without --commit or --dry-run, when the generated file differs GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}, Git Data reads and writes for one commit on checkowners/reconcile-codeowners, then GET, POST, or PATCH /repos/{owner}/{repo}/pulls Repository name, the CODEOWNERS text, and the pull-request body. This call does not use the github extra.

A workflow that posts GITHUB_OUTPUT to a webhook does that itself. checkOwners does not open that connection. See Data flow. The sync row above is the exception to the github extra: it uses the standard library.

docs.title: What is stored
docs.text:
Location Contents ~/.checkowners/state/<id>.json Inferred owners, the analyzed commit, and a history baseline of commit SHAs, path lists, and blame line counts. The baseline does not store author addresses. Email addresses on the ownership map are email: tokens: email: plus the first 16 hex characters of SHA-256 over the lowercased address. ~/.checkowners/graph/<id>.json Serialized ownership graph for that analysis. Contributor emails in node ids are the same tokens. ~/.checkowners/handles/<id>.json This repository's email token to GitHub @handle. A hit stores the handle, the source, and the account type. A miss stores an empty handle and the UTC instant it expires. A legacy string handle is still a hit. A legacy empty string is dropped. @handles are stored as themselves. ~/.checkowners/identity/<id>.json Contributor records for merges and unmerges. Emails are tokens. Handles stay handles. ~/.checkowners/handles.json Legacy global handle file. It is not copied into the per-repository files. cache purge deletes it.

checkowners cache path prints the directory. CHECKOWNERS_STATE_DIR overrides it. The composite Action sets that variable to ~/.checkowners when cache is "true", and to ${{ runner.temp }}/checkowners-state when cache is "false". Analysis does not upload file contents. With cache "true", the Actions cache stores the directory for the next run.

The cache holds hashed emails and @handles. It does not hold raw addresses after the next read. Those identities are still personal data.

docs.title: Deleting it
docs.text:
checkowners cache clear removes analysis state and graph files and leaves handle files and the identity graph in place.

checkowners cache purge removes every file under the cache directory, including per-repository handle files, the identity graph, and a legacy handles.json. That is how you delete this data. The cache directory itself is kept.

docs.title: Disable identity lookup
docs.text: Set github.resolve_handles: false, or pass --offline. Noreply parsing and .mailmap still run locally when mailmap is enabled. --offline also skips review coverage and team verification.

docs.title: Redact emails
docs.text: Set privacy.redact_emails: true, or pass --redact-emails. Addresses in output are replaced with email: tokens. The other presentation controls are in Privacy controls.

docs.title: Retention
docs.text:
There is no time-to-live.

State and graph files are dropped oldest-first once they exceed 256 MiB together. Handle files and the identity graph are not part of that eviction. They stay until cache purge, or until you delete the cache directory.

--max-age SECONDS refuses to reuse an analysis older than that. It does not delete the file. 0 expires immediately for reuse. Omit the flag for no age limit.

A job that uses the Action's runner temp directory loses the cache when the runner is discarded. CLI and hand-rolled CI keep ~/.checkowners/ until you purge it, unless you point CHECKOWNERS_STATE_DIR at an ephemeral path.

docs.text:

    identity[identity resolution]
    reviewApi[review coverage API]
    teamApi[team resolution API]
    localOut[terminal and files]
    githubOutput[GITHUB_OUTPUT]

Identity resolution is local first: a configured identity, .mailmap, GitHub noreply addresses, then this repository's handle file. A commit lookup sends a SHA and reads author.login and account type. User search still sends the email and is last. Org membership is one members request when github.org is set. docs.title: Threat model
docs.text:
What source data is read? Git history, blame, mailmap, ignore-revs, gitattributes, CODEOWNERS, and .github/checkowners.yml. Source file contents are not uploaded.

What leaves the machine? Nothing under --offline, with no token, or without the github extra. Otherwise the calls in What leaves the machine: an unresolved email on user search, repository and pull-request metadata for review coverage, organization and team membership for team resolution, and the report body when the Action comments.

When is GitHub contacted? Only when a gate above is on, GITHUB_TOKEN is set, and the github extra is installed. Local noreply parsing, mailmap, and cache hits do not contact GitHub.

What is cached? The ownership map, the ownership graph, and the handle map, under ~/.checkowners/ or CHECKOWNERS_STATE_DIR.

Does the cache contain sensitive identities? Yes. Emails are email: tokens, not raw addresses. @handles are stored in full. Treat the directory as personal data.

Where is it stored? On the machine that ran the command. The Action uses the runner temp directory. Do not commit the cache. This repo's .gitignore ignores .checkowners/.

How are tokens handled? The only supported token source is the GITHUB_TOKEN environment variable. github.token in config is rejected because that file is committed. See SECURITY.md.

What permissions are required? Job token scopes are in What token scopes are needed. Copy-paste blocks for the Action are in GitHub Actions.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: Full configuration, scoring, and CI reference. The README opens with a drift example, install, and CI. For answers to common questions see docs/FAQ.md.

docs.title: Pipeline
docs.text:
This is a knowledge-risk tool, not a performance-measurement tool. Using it for individual evaluation is unsupported and harmful.

flowchart LR
    Git[Git history] --> Analyze[analyze]
    Analyze --> State[(per-repo state)]
    State --> Generate[generate]
    State --> Drift[drift]
    State --> Owners[qualified-owners]
    State --> Risk[risk]
    State --> Topology[topology]
    State --> Suggest[suggest]
    State --> Onboard[onboard]
    Generate --> CO[CODEOWNERS]
    Drift --> CI[CI output]

State is cached per repo at ~/.checkowners/state/<repo-hash>.json (override the base directory with CHECKOWNERS_STATE_DIR). The hash is the normalized origin URL when the repo has one, so two checkouts of the same remote share a file. A repo with no origin is keyed by its absolute path.

trends is independent of the cached state. It runs its own git log pass and reports historical_activity_confidence (historical-v1), not ownership_score. See Trends. explain and owners (who) also skip the cache. They analyze only the requested file or directory and do not write state.

Downstream commands reuse that file only when its commit is HEAD, its scoring config hash matches, and its model ids match. Otherwise they refresh. A usable baseline replays commits since the stored ref and reuses blame for blobs that did not change. The result matches a full lookback for the same repository, commit, config, and model. Place these flags before the command name:

checkowners --allow-stale decay
checkowners --max-age 86400 qualified-owners
checkowners --no-cache decay
checkowners --no-incremental analyze
checkowners --offline analyze

--allow-stale reuses a map whose commit is not HEAD. --max-age SECONDS refuses a map older than that many seconds (0 expires immediately). Omit it for no age limit. --no-cache neither reads nor writes the analysis cache. --no-incremental scores the full lookback and still writes a fresh baseline. A stored baseline is not used, and the reason is printed, when the scoring config, model ids, schema, repository identity, or package version differ, when the stored commit is missing or is not an ancestor of HEAD, when rename detection changed, when lineage settings changed, or when the baseline does not cover the requested lookback. The first run has no baseline and does not print that notice. --offline makes no network calls and prints:

Network access: disabled
Review evidence: unavailable
Team verification: unavailable

checkowners cache path prints the cache directory. cache info shows size, file counts, each stored commit, blame-cache files, and the current repository: its repo_id, the state file path, and whether that file exists (--json for the same fields). It does not print contributor emails or the ownership map. Exit 0 when that state file exists, exit 1 when this repository has no state file, and exit 2 when the working directory is not a git repository. Both the default ~/.checkowners directory and CHECKOWNERS_STATE_DIR are reported the same way. handles is true when any per-repository handle file or a legacy handles.json is present. cache clear deletes analysis state, graph files, and blame-cache files, and keeps handle files. cache purge deletes everything under the cache directory, including handle files and the identity graph. State, graph, and blame-cache files are evicted oldest-first when they exceed 256 MiB together. Handle files are not evicted; purge deletes them. --verbose prints blame cache: hits=N misses=M on stderr. --no-cache skips blame-cache reads and writes for that run.
